vo: Eight months after launch, a complaint arrives. Customers' ID numbers were collected with no stated reason, kept forever, and shared with a vendor no one checked.
The first question is always the same. Who approved this? Nobody knows.
Because the decision was made here, in a Jira ticket. Created on Tuesday. Shipped on Thursday. Not one privacy question asked.
And South Africa's Information Regulator is fining. One million rand for a major bank. Half a million for a college that shared personal information without a lawful reason.
It keeps happening because one Information Officer can't read four hundred tickets a sprint, and review only happens after the code ships.
So, rewind. Same ticket. Same Tuesday. This time, with Preflight.
The moment someone starts work, Preflight holds the ticket, and says exactly what's missing, and who approves it.
Four questions: the purpose, why less data won't do, the lawful basis, and when it's deleted.
Rovo can draft the answers. But a draft never counts until a person confirms it. AI can help. It can't approve.
The Information Officer sees it in one inbox, reads the answers, and signs off.
Reword the ticket, and it's still caught. Change an approved answer, and the approval goes stale.
Before Done, a second gate asks for proof: the updated privacy notice.
The rules come from your own policy, and nothing is enforced until an approver switches it on.
Eight months later, someone asks the same question. Who approved this? This time, the answer takes ten seconds.
Preflight. Privacy review, before you build.
